subject: research/free-sprtminimax
professional: a sequential-analysis statistician (truncated sequential tests, SPRT / Kiefer-Weiss / 2-SPRT literature); first checks: are the error constraints actually met by the returned policy, is the claimed optimum certified by a dual bound from an independent method, what classical problem is this and is it cited, and how does the new test compare with the classical near-optimal baselines (tuned SPRT, Lorden's 2-SPRT)

evidence.correctness: Every number I recomputed matches by a method the author did not write. (1) Fixed-test sizes 298/181/135 from my own scipy.stats.binom search (indep.py). (2) My own Lagrangian backward-induction DP over deterministic tests (Novikov-style weak duality, Nelder-Mead over the two multipliers) gives the average-objective optimum 98.778 (5%/1%, cap 181) and 66.153 (20%/10%, cap 405), the README's 98.78 and 66.15. (3) The same DP with all weight on one theta gives a lower bound on max_p E_p[N]: 123.79 at theta = 0.0192 for 5%/1% cap 362, equal to the LP minimax value 123.787 (and its p_worst 0.01925), so the LP optimum is certified tight (Weiss's least-favourable-theta structure). (4) Monte Carlo (100k runs per rate) of the subject's minimax policy: P(accept|p0) 0.0497, mean N 70.04 / 123.95 / 110.81 at p = 0.05 / 0.0192 / 0.01 vs 69.9 / 123.8 / 110.8 reported. (5) Re-ran the 20%/10% cap 270 and 5%/1% cap 362 rows of run.py: 66.43, 101.8, 95.2, 63.5/75.8, 6.4% and 86.77, 131.0, 123.8, 69.9/110.8, 5.5%, identical to results.txt.
evidence.completeness: README claims checked: '5 tests, about 10 seconds' (5 passed, 8.05 s); results.txt rows (2 of 15 rerun, identical; other rows consistent with curve.txt and the derived percentages: 1-123.8/181 = 31.6%, 207.6/298 -> 30.3%, 95.2/135 -> 29.5%; design-rate premiums 3.2-5.7%); curve.py/figure.py and mean_vs_p.svg present. Live page https://marisstella.app/research/free-sprtminimax/ could not be loaded (curl returned 000 through the proxy); it is generated from project.json by research/_homepage/registry.py. run.py's full 10-minute rerun not done. No stubs or TODOs.
evidence.verification: `cd research/free-sprtminimax && /usr/bin/python3.13 -m pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider tests`: 5 passed in 8.05 s. Six seeded mutants via platform/ci/quality_mutate.py: 3 caught (P_p1(reject) row built from p0's pmf, sprtminimax.py:72; average objective weighting only p0, :80; flow coefficient f/n scaled 0.999, :53), 3 survived, all in the minimax-specific machinery the headline rests on: cutting-plane refinement disabled (:136), convergence tolerance 1e-3 -> 5.0 (:125), PRUNE 1e-9 -> 1e-5 (:21). The test that 'reproduces the reported worst case' (tests:35) compares r['worst'] with the same worst_case() call that produced it, so it is tautological; no test pins any minimax number or checks LP value vs evaluated worst.
evidence.craft: Read sprtminimax.py (138 lines), tests, run.py, curve.py, figure.py. Clear module docstring deriving the occupation-measure LP; sparse equality matrix; scaling by C(n,f) to keep HiGHS coefficients in range is a thoughtful touch. Defects: minimax() returns silently when the 8 rounds end without the tolerance met (no flag, so the LP value is no longer a certified bound); evaluate() treats any node missing from the policy as reject with no warning; ratio() rebuilds the lgamma list per call; the inequality matrix is built dense then converted; tests import siblings by sys.path insertion; no requirements file (README states numpy/scipy). Acceptable research code.
evidence.claims: Headline numbers all trace to experiments/results.txt and curve.txt and recompute (above); project.json summary and research/README.md:992 match. Limitations are candid (iid Bernoulli twin, worst case over [p1,p0] on a 161-point grid only, randomised tests, pruning). Two soft overclaims: README:29 says the tests check that the policy 'evaluated by an independent forward recursion ... reproduces the reported worst case', but the reported worst case is computed by that same recursion; README:3 frames the question as unasked ('Nobody here had asked') without saying it is the Kiefer-Weiss problem (1957) with a literature of exact and near-optimal solutions.
evidence.fitness: A researcher can rerun everything in seconds to minutes and build on the LP. But nearest prior work is absent: the problem (minimise sup_p E_p[N] subject to error constraints) is the Kiefer-Weiss problem (Kiefer & Weiss 1957; Weiss 1962; Freeman & Weiss 1964 for the binomial; Lorden 1976 2-SPRT, asymptotically optimal; Huffman 1983 algorithms; Novikov 2009 exact truncated tests via backward induction), none cited. The natural practitioner baselines are missing: in my runs (baselines.py, deterministic, boundaries tuned on a 0.05 grid to meet both errors at cap 362) a tuned Wald SPRT has worst-case mean 135.2 and Lorden's 2-SPRT at theta = 0.0192 has 129.0, against 123.8 for the LP and 131.0 for the average-optimal test; so a two-line classical test already beats the average-optimal design, which is exactly the README's open 'next step'. Novelty is low: the LP is a correct computation of a known problem; the numbers for these (p0, p1) pairs are new but not publishable as they stand.
evidence.domain: Against sequential-analysis practice: the method (occupation-measure LP over randomised truncated tests, cutting planes in p) is sound and gives exact, dual-certified optima, which a statistician would accept. Departures: (a) the problem is not named or related to Kiefer-Weiss / modified Kiefer-Weiss theory, so the README misses that its optimum coincides with the modified KW test at the least favourable theta (my single-theta dual equals the minimax value, 123.79 vs 123.787), which explains its own finding that p_worst sits between the rates; (b) no SPRT or 2-SPRT baseline, the comparison a reviewer asks for first; (c) the worst case is certified only on a 161-point grid. A senior statistician would sign off the numbers but not the paper framing.

defects.what: No test covers the minimax-specific machinery: disabling cutting-plane refinement, loosening the convergence tolerance to 5.0 or raising PRUNE to 1e-5 all leave the 5 tests green. The 'reproduces the reported worst case' test compares worst_case() with itself. A test pinning the 20%/10% cap-202 minimax worst (95.3) and asserting worst - value <= 1e-3 would catch all three.

The problem is the (truncated) Kiefer-Weiss problem; Kiefer & Weiss 1957, Weiss 1962, Freeman & Weiss 1964 (binomial), Lorden 1976 (2-SPRT), Huffman 1983 and Novikov 2009 are not cited, and the README's open next step (a two-line-boundary test near the minimax value) is Lorden's 2-SPRT, which in my run reaches 129.0 against 123.8 (5%/1%, cap 362).

No SPRT or 2-SPRT baseline: the only comparisons are the fixed test and the average-optimal test; a tuned SPRT (135.2) and 2-SPRT (129.0) are what a practitioner would otherwise use and bound how much the LP actually buys (4%, not 5.5%, over the best simple rule at cap 362).
README says the tests check the policy's worst case by an independent forward recursion; the 'reported worst case' is produced by that same recursion, so the check is tautological.
minimax() returns silently if 8 rounds end without worst - value <= tol; the result then carries no certificate and no flag.

verdict: Correct and exact: an independent Lagrangian backward-induction DP reproduces the average-optimal values (98.778, 66.153) and certifies the minimax value as optimal (single-theta dual 123.79 vs LP 123.787 at p = 1.92%), Monte Carlo confirms the policy's errors and means, and two results.txt rows rerun identically. It misses the bar on verification: 3 of 6 seeded bugs, all in the cutting-plane minimax code the headline rests on, survive the 5 tests, and the worst-case test is tautological. As research it is a careful computation of the classical Kiefer-Weiss problem without naming it or comparing with Lorden's 2-SPRT, which already gets within 4% (129.0 vs 123.8) and beats the average-optimal test; novelty is low and a sequential-analysis reviewer would ask for that literature and baseline first.
